persons.name: J. W. Reed
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED MAN ON A RECONSTRUCTED ROOF. The papers name him and this household's dwelling does not: what is attested is the person and his trade, and what remains the reconstruction's is everything about where he lived. He is printed as 'J. W. REED.' and the corpus reads his trade as cabinet maker. Cited at the Democrat of 31 December 1833, column 2. THIS ROOF DID NOT COME FROM HIS RECORD. The household was raised by the occupation census because the town of 3,265 people in 398 dwellings needed a joiner and no documented one was available; the register (data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json, action `replace_invented`) is what says one now is. The dwelling's existence, position and footprint are unchanged and still conjectural, and nothing here claims he slept in it — only that the town's need for this trade is met by a man the papers name rather than by one this project invented. The invented name this record used to carry, and its name_basis block, are retired: an invented name is not kept beside a documented one. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1); the placement is L205. He is placed nowhere in particular by his own record, which is the condition of taking ANY roof of his trade — a man the papers put on a named street takes only a roof the plat stands on that street (T-0367), and one they place somewhere this scene cannot honour is refused outright. READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Reed, James W.” (poll_1834_092, line 261); Poll list of 1835 — “Reed, J.W.” (poll_1835_062, line 349). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Reed' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 3 times, as “REED JAMES W”, 1833-10-25: 3 parcels of the school section — lot 1 of block 120 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 5 of block 49 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 8 of block 120 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $507.00 (ls0325, ls0326, ls0327). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: REED JAMES W matches J. W. Reed: the forename names J. W. Reed of the 4 people of this surname, and the forename agrees as an initial only. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD - second of 2 joiner households in this layer, in the north division. The finish half of the building trade - doors, sash, stairs, counters and shop fronts - which the reconstruction schedule names in the same family as the carpenter (W2, 'carpenter or joiner shop') and which the documented layer does not hold at all. A town raising two-storey stores with glazed fronts on South Water and Lake employs men who do nothing else. METHOD: the count comes from the occupation census in data/reconstruction/1835_inferred_household_programme.json, which calibrates every trade against three things this project already holds - the 1835 town census (3,265 people, 398 dwellings), Andreas's roster of the fall of 1833 (about fifty named people, most with a trade, in a settlement of some 350), and the reconstruction specification's roof schedule, whose workshop and store family targets are treated as the ceiling on a trade rather than as its measure. Every count is stated NET of the documented layer: this dataset infers a tradesman only where it cannot name one. RETIRED AN INVENTED NAME (T-0264). This household was raised by the occupation census and named from the invented-name pools. The newspaper register matched it to J. W. Reed, a documented joiner the corpus names 1 time(s) and places nowhere in particular, and he now holds the roof. What changed is WHO: the argument for the household, its dwelling and its position are untouched and still the reconstruction's, and the person's grade is `inferred` — a real man with reconstructed details — rather than `attested`, which would claim the dwelling too. tools/replace_invented_residents.py derives this deal and prints every candidate it refused. T-0489: reconstructed occupancy retired; evidence-based person retained and unplaced.

The papers print 'Joter, Johnson' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 5 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. residents.basis: BEDS, AND ONE FAMILY. 8 of the people here took a bed and are not kin to each other or to anybody else under this roof — `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one record holds them all. persons.name: Stephen II. Preston
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Preston Stephen II.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 5 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 4 February 1834 and nothing says when they came. citations.citation: Chicago · July 1835: Building Inventory and Architectural Reconstruction Specification. Prepared for Kevin Haas, August 2026.
what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED / GENERATED, NOT AN ATTESTED NAMED BUILDING. Aggregate mix follows the supplied specification; exact presence, position, footprint, finish and instance-level form are interpretive. H2 boarding-house massing currently uses a generic rectangular frame block because no boarding-house generator is implemented.

fabric_basis.words: ochre-washed clapboard on a balloon frame under a new roof — a merchant's or professional house, new-built (rule F-M: a merchant's or professional man's by its type)

sizes.upper_windows: ceil(21 crowded beds / 3 to a chamber) = 7, held to 5-10 (the house's own five bays to the H3 crosswalk's top) = 7: 7 across the upper storey of the front and of the rear
sizes.stovepipes: ceil(9 ordinary beds / 3 to a stove) = 3, held to 2-6: 3
sizes.chimneys: not sized by the beds: the two brick stacks are the household's kitchen and common-room hearths, and the stoves the beds add go out through the roof as stovepipes

lodging.note: The town model puts a boarding house at 9 people on an ordinary night and 21 when full, from the 1840 household tail (p90 and p99 of 964 Chicago households). This building takes the share of its class's total that its 198 m² of enclosed floor (99 m² × 2 storeys) is of the class's floor area.
lodging.replaceable_by: Any source that states this house's rooms, beds or lodgers on a dated day: an advertisement counting its rooms, a traveller's account of how many it slept, a licence return. A stated capacity retires the apportioned one outright.

occupancy.statement: 9 on this card against an ordinary night's 9 beds: 1 seated here from elsewhere in the layer, where no source gives them a roof, 7 drawn against the order book's lodging buckets for beds that were standing empty, a keeper drawn for a roof this programme raised.
occupancy.keeper_owed: Minted by this stage as the keeper. T-1533 drew this keeper's own children here — 2 of them — out of the book's `under_10` lodging cells, at the size the 1840 histogram gives the household. What is still owed is a SPOUSE, which no rule this project has made can draw for a keeper who is a woman; the ledger's `keeper_families` row states it, and the staffing under a keeper is T-1183's.
